name: Gerard Mercator, Nova et aucta orbis terrae descriptio, 1569 — sheet 4 (North Atlantic)
holding: Maritiem Museum Prins Hendrik facsimile (Imago Mundi supplement 2), via Wikimedia Commons
note: 10930x8370 TIF, converted to JPEG for tracing. Mercator's own projection, so the sheet carries a usable graticule: a meridian bar ruled in alternating one-degree segments runs down the sheet right beside S. Brandain, with the 60th parallel labelled. Chosen in October 2026 for the northern Saint-Brendan — the island of the Navigatio, as the printed atlases carried it west of Ireland — over Honorius Philoponus 1621 (the whale engraving: an illustration, not a chart) and Delisle 1707 (the Canarian San Borondón, a 35 px blob). Mercator 1569 is the most influential printed depiction of this tradition; Ortelius copied it.

graticule.ladder_note: One-degree segments on the meridian bar at x~4440, read at full resolution. The 60th parallel is ruled across at y=5513. Fit y = c - R*ln(tan(45+lat/2)) to the eleven boundaries 60..50 N: R = 4740.9 px/rad (82.74 px per degree of longitude), RMS 3.3 px. The segments shrink from 160 to 126 px going south exactly as the projection requires, which is how it is known they are degrees.

longitude_landmarks_note: LONGITUDE ONLY, and deliberately not under "landmarks", so trace_outline.py takes the manual path. Mercator's longitudes are counted from his own prime meridian, so the offset is fitted on the nearest real coast instead, with the scale held at the graticule's. Eight points on Ireland, Wales and Cornwall: offset s.d. 0.54 degrees; latitudes from the ladder land within 5-53 km of true. S. Brandain is 1465 px west of the Blaskets, but along a Mercator parallel that is pure graticule, not an extrapolated fit: only the offset is borrowed.
